lead: A flat slab is a slab carried straight on columns, with no beams. The floor load goes from the slab into the columns, so the slab is often thickened round each column with a drop, and the column top may be widened into a capital. Flat slabs give a flat ceiling, a lower storey height and simple formwork, which suits offices, malls, hospitals and car parks. IS 456 clause 31 designs a regular layout by the direct design method and checks punching shear round every column.
prereq: You need Two-way slabs with various edge conditions (two-way bending) and the shear strength of slabs.

items: Flat plate: a slab of uniform thickness on plain columns, for light loads and short spans.
Drop: a thickening of the slab round the column, rectangular in plan and at least one-third of the panel length in each direction. It adds depth where the hogging moment and shear are largest.
Column head (capital): a flared top of the column. Only the part inside a 90° cone or pyramid fitting within the column and head counts in design.

Column strip: the band along a column line, 0.25l₂ wide on each side of the line but not more than 0.25l₁ (l₁ is the span being designed, l₂ the span across it). The middle strip is the rest of the panel width.
Thickness: at least 125 mm. The span/d rules of cl. 23.2 apply directly to slabs with drops; without drops they are multiplied by 0.9. Use the longer span.

blocks.text: The method may be used when there are at least three continuous spans each way, panels are rectangular with long/short span ≤ 2, successive spans differ by no more than one-third of the longer, columns are offset by at most 10 % of the span, and the live load is not more than three times the dead load. Then each direction is designed for the total static moment of one panel:

blocks.where: W = w<sub>u</sub> l₂ lₙ is the total design load on the panel width l₂ over the clear span lₙ (kN). lₙ runs between the faces of the columns or capitals, but is not taken less than 0.65l₁. M₀ is in kN·m for the whole panel width.

blocks.text: End spans use other fractions that depend on how stiff the outer column is, and the column strip takes all of the negative moment at an exterior support. Divide each strip moment by the strip width to get a moment per metre, then design the steel as for a one-way slab, with the depth of the drop at the column. Layouts that fail the conditions are designed by the equivalent frame method (cl. 31.5).

A column can punch through the slab along a truncated cone or pyramid. The critical section is a perimeter at d/2 from the face of the column, capital or drop, and the shear on it is the load on the panel outside that perimeter. The stress must not exceed k<sub>s</sub> τ<sub>c</sub>, where τ<sub>c</sub> = 0.25√f<sub>ck</sub> and k<sub>s</sub> = 0.5 + β<sub>c</sub> ≤ 1 (β<sub>c</sub> = short side/long side of the column). Above that, up to 1.5 times it, shear reinforcement is needed; beyond that the slab must be made deeper or given a drop or capital. When a drop is used, check a second perimeter at d/2 outside the drop, where the slab is thinner.

examples.question: An interior panel of a flat slab floor is 6.0 m × 6.0 m with 450 mm square columns. Slab 200 mm, drops 2.0 m × 2.0 m with total depth 250 mm. Live load 4 kN/m², finish 1 kN/m², M20. Find the strip moments by the direct design method and check punching shear.
steps: Conditions: three or more spans each way (assumed), square panels, live load 4 < 3 × dead load. Drop 2.0 m ≥ 6.0/3 = 2.0 m.
Loads: slab 0.200 × 25 = 5.00; drops averaged over the panel 0.05 × 25 × 4/36 = 0.139; finish 1.0; live 4.0; w = 10.139 kN/m², w<sub>u</sub> = 15.208 kN/m².
Strips: column strip 2 × 0.25 × 6.0 = 3.0 m; middle strip 3.0 m.

Per metre: column strip negative 0.75 × 228.4/3.0 = 57.1; middle strip negative 0.25 × 228.4/3.0 = 19.0; column strip positive 0.60 × 123.0/3.0 = 24.6; middle strip positive 0.40 × 123.0/3.0 = 16.4 kN·m/m.

Punching at the column: d at the drop ≈ 250 − 35 = 215 mm; perimeter side 450 + 215 = 665 mm, b₀ = 2660 mm. V<sub>u</sub> = 15.208 × (36 − 0.665²) = 540.8 kN; τ<sub>v</sub> = 540774/(2660 × 215) = 0.946 N/mm². k<sub>s</sub> = 1 (square column), τ<sub>c</sub> = 0.25√20 = 1.118 N/mm². Safe.
Punching outside the drop: d = 200 − 35 = 165 mm; side 2000 + 165 = 2165 mm; V<sub>u</sub> = 15.208 × (36 − 2.165²) = 476.2 kN; τ<sub>v</sub> = 0.333 N/mm². Safe.
Without the drop the 200 mm slab gives τ<sub>v</sub> = 1.33 N/mm² at the column, more than 1.118 (but under 1.5 × 1.118 = 1.68): it would need shear reinforcement. That is why the drop is used.
Thickness: 6000/165 = 36.4; with the column strip mid-span steel (p<sub>t</sub> ≈ 0.26 %) the factor is about 1.56, so the limit is 26 × 1.56 = 40.6. Safe.
examples.answer: M₀ = 351.3 kN·m; column strip 57.1 (negative) and 24.6 (positive) kN·m/m; middle strip 19.0 and 16.4 kN·m/m. Punching τ<sub>v</sub> = 0.95 and 0.33 N/mm², both under 1.12 N/mm².

traps: Using the centre-to-centre span in M₀. lₙ is the clear span between column faces (not less than 0.65l₁), and W is the load on l₂ × lₙ.
Quoting M₀ or a strip moment as kN·m per metre. Divide by the strip width first.
Making the column strip the full panel width. It is 0.25l₂ each side of the column line (here 3.0 m in all).
Checking punching only at the column face. The section is at d/2 from the face, and a second check is needed outside the drop.
Using the beam τ<sub>c</sub> of Table 19 for punching. Flat slabs use τ<sub>c</sub> = 0.25√f<sub>ck</sub> times k<sub>s</sub>.

quiz.a: A reinforced concrete slab carried directly by columns, without beams, often with drops and column heads.

quiz.q: State the minimum size of a drop and the minimum thickness of a flat slab.
quiz.a: Drop at least one-third of the panel length in each direction; slab at least 125 mm thick.

quiz.q: Why does the column strip take 75 % of the negative moment?
quiz.a: The band along the column line is much stiffer near the column, so it attracts most of the hogging moment and must deliver it to the column.

quiz.q: A panel has l₂ = 5.0 m, lₙ = 4.6 m and w<sub>u</sub> = 12 kN/m². Find M₀.
For M₀ = 200 kN·m in an interior span 6 m wide, find the column strip negative moment per metre.
quiz.a: Negative 0.65 × 200 = 130 kN·m; column strip 0.75 × 130 = 97.5 kN·m over 3.0 m = 32.5 kN·m/m.

quiz.q: A flat plate is safe in bending but cracks round a column under full load. What was missed and what are the fixes?
quiz.a: Punching shear at d/2 from the column face. Add a drop or capital, thicken the slab, or provide shear reinforcement (stirrups or shear studs) if τ<sub>v</sub> is under 1.5k<sub>s</sub>τ<sub>c</sub>.

beyond: Not for the exam. Many flat slabs are now post-tensioned to control deflection over 8 to 10 m spans, and punching is resisted with stud rails. Collapses of flat slabs through progressive punching have led codes to ask for integrity bars running continuously through the columns. Search for "punching shear studs" and "post-tensioned flat slab".

figure.caption: One interior panel of the worked example: the shaded bands are the halves of the column strips along the column lines, the centre band the middle strip. Dashed outlines show the 2.0 m drops and the punching perimeters at d/2 from each column; both punching stresses stay under 1.12 N/mm².
